summary:
Mississippi stands under the national framework of the United States, which applies in full. The findings below are what the state adds, and where state practice differs, on top of that framework.

The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update places Mississippi in its "Worst Laws Passed" category, among states the assessment describes as having legislatively erased transgender people. That grading derives from a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric.

Facility access is restricted by state law. A measure signed 13 May 2024 and effective immediately requires individuals in public schools to use bathrooms consistent with sex "determined solely by birth." The Movement Advancement Project tabulates Mississippi as having enacted bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity in 2024 and 2025, and records that state statute defines sex by birth.

Identity documents carry an outing risk of their own. Mississippi's Vital Records office issues an amended birth certificate with a new name and gender marker on presentation of a certified court order, a medical statement attesting to gender reassignment and a fee, but the certificate lists both the updated and the original information, so the prior marker stays on the document. Driver's licence sex markers could be changed on a Gender Designation Form signed by a physician or psychotherapist from 1 November 2021 until a March 2026 law prohibited markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth.

On 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a transgender teen undergoing gender transition cannot change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented. The majority opinion, written by Justice James D. Maxwell II, referred to the trans boy as a "minor female" and cited the 2023 REAP Act as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving life-altering gender-transition assistance; a chancellor may grant a minor's name change only where clearly in the child's best interest.

Gender-affirming care for individuals under 18 is banned under the Regulate Experimental Adolescent Procedures (REAP) Act, signed 28 February 2023. The University of Mississippi Medical Center's TEAM Clinic closed on 30 June 2023, leaving Spectrum: The Other Clinic in Hattiesburg operating virtually as the only LGBTQ+-specializing clinic in the state.

Mississippi's 1994 state hate-crime statute does not include gender identity. Federal prosecution remains available, and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Mississippi reported that Joshua Brandon Vallum was sentenced to 49 years in federal prison for the bias-motivated murder of a transgender woman in Lucedale. That sentence was handed down in 2017; the most recent documented bias-motivated killing of a trans person in Mississippi in this material is from 2017, and no later instance is documented.

The Religious Liberty Accommodations Act (HB 1523), effective after the Fifth Circuit lifted an injunction on 23 June 2017, protects individuals, religious organisations and some businesses acting on beliefs that include that gender is determined at birth by anatomy and genetics, giving providers a statutory basis for refusing service.

State non-discrimination law provides no protection based on gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations. Jackson, Clarksdale, Holly Springs and Magnolia ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Hattiesburg, Oxford and Starkville protect city employees only.

Same-sex marriages are recognised in Mississippi under the nationwide rule. The state's own instruments, a 1996 executive order, a 1997 statutory ban and 2004 constitutional Amendment 1 approved by 86.01% of voters, remain unrepealed; on 29 June 2015 Attorney General Jim Hood directed clerks to comply with recognition or face lawsuits, after initial resistance in some counties. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship is therefore recognised in law while the state's contrary instruments stay on the books.

An enacted measure prohibits name changes for people in state custody. The Real You Act of 2022, which would have permitted them, died in committee.
tangentialFactors:
Two restrictive bills died in the 2024 session without a vote. The "SAFER Act," which would have restricted transgender people's use of public bathrooms, locker rooms and public university dormitories and had earlier backing from a House majority, and the "Women's Bill of Rights," which would have codified a binary definition of sex determined at birth and curtailed legal recognition of transgender people's gender identities, both lapsed when House and Senate lawmakers failed to agree on compromise versions by the 29 April 2024 deadline.

Public opinion in the state is measured rather than trans-specific. A 2019 PRRI poll found 68% of Mississippians favoured laws protecting gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people from discrimination in jobs, housing and public accommodations, with 23% opposed; PRRI reported that by 2024 support for a statewide anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity reached 67%. The source states that Mississippi shows lower support than national averages for same-sex marriage and transgender rights, that opinion gaps have narrowed over time, and that younger residents show significantly higher support than older residents.

Visible community presence exists alongside the statutory picture. Starkville held its first pride parade on 24 March 2018 after an initial permit denial, drawing approximately 3,000 participants and becoming the largest parade in the city's history.
localsOnly:
State law bars transgender students from school sports consistent with their gender identity under SB 2536, signed 11 March 2021 and effective 1 July 2021. Where an athlete's sex is disputed, the statute requires a physician's statement verifying genitalia, DNA and hormone levels.

A 2024 Harrison County dress code requiring clothing to match sex assigned at birth led to a transgender girl being threatened with in-school suspension for wearing a dress to a regional band event.

Residents seeking a corrected birth certificate must obtain a certified court order and a medical statement and pay a fee, and the resulting certificate carries both the updated and the original information. Driver's licence marker changes were available between 1 November 2021 and March 2026 and are no longer available under the March 2026 law.

Employment, housing and public accommodations protections on gender identity exist only in the four municipalities with full ordinances and, on an employment basis only, in three others; the remainder of the state has no such statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
The two accounts of the April 2025 name-change ruling in this material do not match. One reports that the Mississippi Supreme Court denied the petition outright on 17 April 2025; the other states the court barred the change until age 21 for "lack of maturity." Which formulation reflects the operative holding is unresolved here.

The Movement Advancement Project's tally places Mississippi's facility bans in 2024 and 2025, but the specific 2025 enactment counted, and its scope beyond schools, are not identified in this material.

No enforcement data is sourced on how the facility restrictions are applied to adults, including visitors, in practice. No documented arrest of an adult under the 2024 provision appears here.

The March 2026 law barring licence markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth is not sourced as to its exceptions, transition provisions, or its treatment of licences issued by other states.

Whether the dual listing on an amended Mississippi birth certificate appears on the certified copies used to support travel or identity documents is not sourced.

No survey of Mississippi trans people's own reported experiences in a recent period is present in this material; the opinion figures cited cover the state population generally and are dated 2019 and 2024.
